summary:
Père David's Deer — known in China as Milu — once roamed the wetlands and river valleys of eastern China, an elegant and unusual deer whose very survival depended on the mercy of strangers. With its distinctive branching antlers and semi-aquatic habits, it evolved across millennia before habitat loss and hunting quietly erased it from the wild.

What remained was rescued, improbably, through captive breeding programs in Beijing and beyond. By 1993, only 120 individuals survived. Today, over 2,000 live in protected facilities — a fragile second chance shadowed by low genetic diversity and an uncertain homeland. The wild places that once held them may no longer exist.
